outputs.L2: A process for producing a three-dimensional article includes the following steps: first, placing a layer of particulate material on a build plate; next, directing a first laser beam, defined by a first group of beam parameters, onto the particulate layer so that the layer is heated enough to join at least some of the particles and create a build layer; then, applying a second laser beam, having a second group of beam parameters, to a first area of either the particulate layer or the build layer so as to establish a first temperature distribution in that first area; and further, applying a third laser beam, having a third group of beam parameters, to a second area of either the particulate layer or the build layer so as to establish a second temperature distribution in that second area, where the second temperature distribution differs from the first. The first and second areas are both located either within the particulate layer or within the build layer.

A method of forming a three-dimensional object includes positioning a layer of particles over a build plate. The layer of particles may be distributed across the build plate to define a surface on which a portion of the object is to be formed.

A first laser beam is then directed onto the particle layer. The first laser beam heats the particles to a temperature sufficient to fuse at least some of the particles together, thereby forming a build layer. The fused particles define at least a portion of the three-dimensional object being produced.

In addition to the first laser beam, a second laser beam is directed onto a first region of either the particle layer or the build layer. The second laser beam exposes the first region in a manner that produces a first temperature profile within that region.

A third laser beam is directed onto a second region of the same type of layer exposed by the second laser beam. For example, if the second laser beam exposes a region of the particle layer, the third laser beam also exposes another region of the particle layer. Similarly, if the second laser beam exposes a region of the build layer, the third laser beam also exposes another region of the build layer. The third laser beam produces a second temperature profile within the second region.

The second temperature profile is different from the first temperature profile. As a result, different regions of the particle layer or build layer may be thermally controlled in different ways during formation of the three-dimensional object.

A method is provided for fabricating a three-dimensional object using a powder-based additive manufacturing process. In the method, a layer of particulate build material is deposited onto a build plate or onto a previously formed layer of the object. The particulate material may include metal, polymer, ceramic, composite, or another fusible material suitable for additive manufacturing. After the layer is spread to a desired thickness, selected portions of the layer are exposed to laser energy to fuse, melt, sinter, or otherwise consolidate the particles according to a digital model of the object being produced.

A first laser is directed onto the layer to form a primary fused region. This laser may be configured to provide the main energy input required to join the particles and create the structural portion of the build layer. The first laser can be scanned across the powder bed along a predetermined toolpath, thereby defining the geometry of the object for that layer. Once the selected areas have been processed, additional layers of particulate material may be deposited and fused in a similar manner until the three-dimensional object is completed.

In addition to the first laser, one or more additional lasers are selectively applied to different regions of the same layer, to different areas within a single melt pool, or to different portions of an individual particle or group of particles. These additional lasers may have beam characteristics that differ from those of the first laser. For example, the lasers may differ in wavelength, power, beam diameter, spot shape, pulse duration, pulse frequency, polarization, scan speed, angle of incidence, or energy distribution. A secondary laser may be broader and lower in power to preheat a region, while another may be more focused to increase local melting, refine microstructure, or control cooling behavior. In some implementations, one laser may be continuous-wave while another is pulsed, allowing the system to apply different types of thermal energy to different regions of the build material.

By coordinating the operation of the first laser and the additional lasers, the method creates distinct temperature profiles in separate regions of the same build layer. For instance, one region may be heated to a temperature sufficient to fully melt the particles, while an adjacent region may be maintained at a lower temperature to reduce thermal gradients, prevent cracking, or control residual stress. In another example, a leading laser beam may preheat powder before the primary fusion beam reaches it, and a trailing laser beam may slow the cooling rate after fusion. The additional laser energy may also be applied only to selected features, such as thin walls, overhangs, edges, corners, high-stress regions, or areas requiring specific material properties.

The ability to generate different localized temperature profiles provides improved thermal control during the additive manufacturing process. Localized thermal management can help reduce defects such as porosity, warping, delamination, balling, incomplete fusion, and undesirable microstructural variation. It may also allow different portions of the object to be manufactured with different mechanical, thermal, or metallurgical properties. For example, one region of a component may be processed to have high hardness, while another region may be processed to have improved ductility or reduced residual stress.

The lasers may be controlled by a processing system that receives data from a digital part model and determines where and when each laser is applied. The processing system may also use sensor feedback, such as thermal imaging, pyrometry, optical monitoring, or melt-pool measurements, to adjust the laser parameters in real time. Based on the sensed temperature or melt-pool condition, the system can modify laser power, scanning pattern, exposure time, or beam size to maintain a desired temperature profile in each region.

In this manner, the method enables a single additive manufacturing build layer, or even a single localized region within that layer, to be processed using multiple laser beams having different thermal effects. The result is a three-dimensional object formed layer by layer with enhanced control over heat input, cooling rate, microstructure, and final material properties. This localized laser-based thermal control can improve part quality, increase process reliability, and expand the range of materials and geometries that can be produced using additive manufacturing.

**The Power of “The”**

The word **“the”** may seem small and ordinary, but it is one of the most important words in the English language. It is called a definite article, and it helps us talk about something specific. For example, when we say “the book,” we do not mean just any book—we mean a particular book that the speaker and listener understand.

“The” gives clarity to our sentences. It points to a known person, place, object, or idea. In phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” or “the truth,” the word helps create a sense of importance and uniqueness. Without it, many sentences would feel incomplete or unclear.

Although it has only three letters, “the” appears everywhere in English writing and speech. It connects ideas smoothly and makes communication more precise. This simple word proves that even the smallest parts of language can have a powerful role.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate claim language for a 3D printing process in which particles are positioned over a build plate, fused with one laser, and separate regions of either the powder layer or build layer are exposed to additional laser beams to produce different temperature profiles.
counterfactuals.output:
1. **A method of additively manufacturing a three-dimensional article, the method comprising:**

   depositing a layer of particulate build material over a build plate;

   selectively irradiating a first region of the layer with a first laser beam to fuse particles of the particulate build material in the first region and thereby form at least a portion of a build layer of the three-dimensional article; and

   exposing a second region, different from the first region, to a second laser beam to establish a first temperature profile in the second region,

   wherein the second region comprises at least one of an unfused region of the layer of particulate build material or a previously fused region of the build layer, and

   wherein exposing the second region to the second laser beam is performed independently of the selective irradiation with the first laser beam such that different regions of the layer or build layer are provided with different temperature profiles.

2. **The method of claim 1**, further comprising exposing a third region, different from the first and second regions, to a third laser beam to establish a second temperature profile different from the first temperature profile.

3. **The method of claim 2**, wherein the second laser beam and the third laser beam have different power levels, scan speeds, spot sizes, dwell times, pulse durations, wavelengths, or combinations thereof.

4. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the second laser beam heats the second region without substantially fusing particles in the second region.

5. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the second laser beam preheats an unfused powder region before the first laser beam fuses particles in the unfused powder region.

6. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the second laser beam reheats, anneals, stress relieves, or controls cooling of a fused region of the build layer after fusion by the first laser beam.

7. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the first laser beam is operated at an energy density sufficient to melt or sinter the particulate build material, and the second laser beam is operated at an energy density insufficient to fully melt the particulate build material.

8. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the different temperature profiles comprise different peak temperatures, heating rates, cooling rates, thermal gradients, dwell times above a threshold temperature, or combinations thereof.

9. **The method of claim 1**, further comprising controlling the second laser beam based on a location of the second region relative to a boundary of the three-dimensional article, an overhang, a support structure, a heat accumulation region, or a previously solidified portion of the article.

10. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the second region is laterally spaced from the first region within a common layer of particulate build material.

11. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the second region vertically overlaps the first region and comprises a portion of a previously formed build layer beneath the layer of particulate build material.

12. **The method of claim 1**, further comprising repeating the depositing, selectively irradiating, and exposing steps for a plurality of layers to form the three-dimensional article.

13. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the first laser beam and the second laser beam are generated by separate laser sources.

14. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the first laser beam and the second laser beam are generated from a common laser source and directed along different optical paths.

15. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the second laser beam is scanned over the second region according to a thermal-management scan pattern different from a fusion scan pattern of the first laser beam.

16. **The method of claim 1**, wherein exposing the second region to the second laser beam reduces residual stress, distortion, porosity, cracking, or microstructural variation in the three-dimensional article.

17. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the particulate build material comprises metal powder, ceramic powder, polymer powder, composite powder, or combinations thereof.

18. **A method of controlling thermal conditions during powder-bed additive manufacturing, the method comprising:**

   forming a powder layer over a build plate;

   scanning a fusion laser beam over selected portions of the powder layer to form fused portions of a build layer; and

   concurrently or sequentially scanning at least one auxiliary laser beam over one or more regions of the powder layer or the build layer that are separate from the selected portions scanned by the fusion laser beam,

   wherein the at least one auxiliary laser beam is controlled to produce region-specific temperature profiles that differ from a temperature profile produced by the fusion laser beam.

19. **The method of claim 18**, wherein the at least one auxiliary laser beam comprises a plurality of auxiliary laser beams respectively directed to different regions of the powder layer or build layer.

20. **The method of claim 18**, wherein the region-specific temperature profiles are selected based on a thermal model, sensed temperature data, build geometry, material composition, or combinations thereof.
